### A1 · Label it

The legend label is the most valuable change; the outcome was not originally listed, and therefore could not be interpreted without access to source code.

### A2 · Choose a scale

```{r}
#| label: fig-a2
#| ref.label: a2
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My scale choice."
#| fig-alt: "Using a log10 scale, we can see what ages of participants make up a majority of our data based on a rough bell curve."
```

```{r}
#| label: a2-check
#| include: false
```

With the log10scale, readers are more clearly able to see the pattern of what ages are most common in the dataset; no values were removed, but now our graph has a far greater shape.

### A3 · Facet it: fixed or free

```{r}
#| label: fig-a3
#| ref.label: a3
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The same rates in panels: fixed and free y-axes."
#| fig-subcap: ["Fixed", "Free"]
#| fig-alt: "The fixed axis graph shows us how the two rates compare; the free y-axis graph, however, simply shows us the rate (disproportionately)."
#| layout: [[1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-chosen
#| include: false
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a3
#| tbl-cap: "Each group's n and rate, by panel."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(a3_rates, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-check
#| include: false
```

The Fixed axis is most accurate. While the free y-axis graph does show the correct markings per graph, it misleads the reader to believe the rate of males and the rate of females with the outcome of 50K or above is near-even. The females panel is roughly half the count of the males panel, at 1657 compared to 3343, and therefore even a minor change in interpretation could be incorrect.

### A4 · Compared to what?

```{r}
#| label: fig-a4
#| ref.label: a4
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Two groups: individual values and resampled means, same axes."
#| fig-alt: "These plots show that those who work more hours a week are spread roughly evenly, but the means of each group are different."
```

```{r}
#| label: a4-check
#| include: false
```

Individual values overlap very frequently, and have similar spread; however, the means show that those who are traditionally married work, on average, more hours per week than those who have never been married.


```{r}
#| label: a5-colors

```

```{r}

```

```{r}
#| label: a5-check

```

I have chosen to colour by sex; this allows the data to be interpreted in the simplest division, where we can see that, based on the previous graph, those who are working around 40hrs/week are primarily married, and in this graph we can see which sex makes up that majority.

## Part B · Sports

### B1 · Label it

```{r}
#| label: fig-b1
#| ref.label: b1
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My Sports plot, labeled for a reader."
#| fig-alt: "The proprotion of how many matches by rounds that judges agree on their decision."
```

```{r}
#| label: b1-check
#| include: false
```

This plot shows different matches, when divided into the amount of rounds per match, and what share of matches end in an "Agreed" decision. However, the most important label here would be the x-axis, because the factored rounds are not likely to be interpreted correctly otherwise.

### B2 · Choose a scale

```{r}
#| label: fig-b2
#| ref.label: b2
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My scale choice."
#| fig-alt: "This plot shows that, based on a continuous scale, what percentage of matches that judge1's score varies by a particular amount from the average (absolute value)"
```

```{r}
#| label: b2-check
#| include: false
```

I went with a continuous scale, as there is not much of a pattern to analyze; instead, a calculation of shares is more important, to see how much higher/lower judge1 voted in a majority of matches, and if they were often in strong agreement.

### B3 · Facet it: fixed or free

```{r}
#| label: fig-b3
#| ref.label: b3
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The same plot in panels: fixed and free y-axes."
#| fig-subcap: ["Fixed", "Free"]
#| fig-alt: "WRITE: one sentence describing the two plots."
#| layout: [[1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: b3-check
#| include: false
```

A fixed scale better represents the percentage of matches that judges agreed on their decision; additionally, 5-round matches are far smaller than 3-round matches, and 12-round matches are even smaller.

### B4 · Compared to what?

```{r}
#| label: fig-b4
#| ref.label: b4
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Two groups: individual values and resampled means, same axes."
#| fig-alt: "The plot shows that there is a far higher spread in unanimous decisions by judge1's score margin, while a split decision is mostly consistent; furthermore, the means also differ.."
```

```{r}
#| label: b4-check
#| include: false
```

Clouds overlap about half of the time; however, this is also due to a higher spread in unanimous decision occurrences. This means individual occurrences are varied highly; additionally, the means are far more condensed, meaning the unanimous decision mean doesnt account for the extremeties as much as the more focused split decision.

### B5 · Color for every reader

```{r}
#| label: fig-b5
#| ref.label: [b5, b5-simulated]
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My colors, with a second cue, and how a reader with red-green color blindness might see them."
#| fig-subcap: ["My plot", "Red-green (deuteranopia), simulated"]
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "This plot shos what percent of matches fall in each result type, divided by three values: Agree, Disagree, and Judge (Grouped where one judge has the primary result decision)"
#|   - "The same plot in the colors a reader with red-green color blindness (deuteranopia) might see."
#| layout-ncol: 2
```

```{r}
#| label: b5-colors
#| echo: true
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-b5-views
#| ref.label: b5-other-views
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The other two simulated views."
#| fig-subcap: ["Red-green (protanopia), simulated", "Blue-yellow (approximate), simulated"]
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "The same plot in the colors a reader with red-green color blindness (protanopia) might see."
#|   - "The same plot in the colors a reader with blue-yellow color blindness might see (an approximation)."
#| layout-ncol: 2
```

```{r}
#| label: b5-check
#| include: false
```

I divided colours based on agreement value; this originally did not work, as the "judge_" value had too few occurrences; therefore, I grouped them into one category, and now it is far easier to tell them apart. I chose this paneling because even those who cannot see any colours will be able to see the three results and tell them apart by labels.
